title: Extreme poverty in India halved to 2.6% in 2023 from year ago: World Bank data
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Siddharth Upasani)
syllabus: GS1 › Poverty and developmental issues; Role of women · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty and hunger · GS3 › Inclusive growth; Employment · GS2 › International institutions (World Bank)
summary: The World Bank's Poverty & Equity Brief puts India's extreme poverty ($3 a day, 2021 PPP) at 2.6% in 2023, but flags wage gaps, regional concentration and low-productivity jobs.
ideas: Fast fall, on every line: extreme poverty fell from 27.1% (2011) to 5.3% (2022-23) and 2.6% (2023); the lower-middle-income line ($4.2) fell from 57.7% to 16.1%, lifting about 496 million people.
GS1 · Poverty
India recorded one of the world's fastest poverty declines, in monetary and non-monetary terms, says the World Bank.
Poverty is now a place, not just a condition: about 57% of India's poor live in one belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal, so further gains depend on productive jobs in these states.
GS1 · Regional disparity / GS3 · Inclusive growth
With poverty concentrated geographically, the next phase of poverty reduction is a question of regional, job-rich growth.
Jobs grew, earnings did not: employment rose by 13.4 crore (2017-2023), led by rural women entering paid work, but real earnings stayed flat and jobs were in low-productivity activities.
GS3 · Employment
Employment growth without real wage growth signals a quantity-quality gap in India's labour market.
Inequality looks lower but may be understated: the consumption Gini fell to 23.0, yet the Bank warns surveys may miss richer households, and the top 10% earn about 13 times the bottom 10%.
GS2 · Poverty / GS3 · Inequality
Falling consumption inequality coexists with sharp wage inequality; survey design may understate the gap at the top.
Lines and measurement matter: the Bank uses three lines ($3, $4.2, $8.3) in 2021 PPP; new Indian survey data have revised global poverty counts before, so methodology shapes the story.
GS2 · International institutions / GS3 · Measurement
Poverty estimates depend on the line, the PPP base and survey design; India's data revisions shift global counts.
keywords: Converts incomes to a common currency after adjusting for price levels
PPP lines measure what money buys, not its exchange value, so poverty comparisons stay meaningful across countries.
Poverty clustering in a few lagging regions
As poverty concentrates geographically, place-based strategies matter more than nationwide schemes.
Being employed yet earning too little to move up
Jobs concentrated in low-productivity work keep many in working poverty.
Women's rising entry into paid work
The rise of rural women in paid work is driving India's employment growth.
The hardest residual poverty, harder to reduce than the first gains
As headline poverty falls, last-mile poverty needs targeted, region-specific interventions.
Gaps in pay can widen even as gaps in spending narrow
Consumption inequality may fall while earnings inequality stays pronounced.
data: Extreme poverty ($3/day, 2021 PPP), down from 5.3% (2022-23) and 27.1% (2011)
Extreme poverty fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023 (World Bank).
Below the $4.2 line, down from 57.7% in 2011: about 496 million lifted out
About 496 million Indians crossed the $4.2-a-day line between 2011 and 2023 (World Bank).
Share of India's poor living in the belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal
Nearly 57% of India's poor live in the UP–West Bengal belt (World Bank).
Rise in employment, 2017-2023, nearly twice the rise in working-age population; led by rural women
Employment grew by 13.4 crore in 2017-23, driven by rural women entering paid work (World Bank).
Median earnings of the top 10% of workers over the bottom 10%
The top 10% of workers earn about 13 times the bottom 10% (World Bank).
Youth unemployment, Q1 of 2025-26 to Q1 of this fiscal
Youth unemployment rose from 14.6% to 15.9% in a year, even as overall jobs grew.
examples: UP–West Bengal poverty belt
Where most of India's remaining poor live
GS1 · Regional disparity / GS3 · Inclusive growth
The UP–West Bengal belt shows why balanced regional development is now central to poverty reduction.
Women Home Guard aspirants, Jharkhand
About 6,000 women ran trials in Ramgarh for 284 Home Guard posts (Big Picture, page 21)
GS4
GS1 · Women and work
Thousands of rural women racing for a few Home Guard posts show both the aspiration and the scarcity of decent jobs.
pyqs: Poverty and unequal ownership of resources: the 13-times wage gap and concentrated poverty fit here.
Why poverty persists despite schemes: regional concentration and low-productivity jobs are fresh reasons.
Incidence and intensity beyond income: the Bank's multiple lines and non-monetary progress.
Is India's growth inclusive: falling poverty with flat real earnings is a two-sided answer.
Labour-led growth vs productivity: jobs grew in low-productivity activities.

trend.t: GS1 asked why poverty persists (2016, 2018) and how COVID deepened it (2020); GS2 moved to measurement (multidimensional poverty, 2020) and to structural causes such as unequal ownership of resources (2025). GS3 keeps asking whether growth is inclusive (2017, 2019, 2022, 2024, 2025).
trend.watch: Inclusive growth is asked almost every year in GS3, and poverty's structural causes keep returning in GS1 and GS2. Know both the numbers and the reasons poverty persists.
focus: Measuring poverty: lines, PPP and multidimensional indices
Why poverty persists: regions, assets and job quality

potential: "Falling poverty in India is increasingly a question of where the poor live and what work they do." Discuss. (15 marks)
India's poverty has declined sharply, yet earnings inequality remains pronounced. Examine the reasons and suggest measures. (10 marks)
Discuss the role of rural women's entry into paid work in India's recent employment growth. What limits its impact on poverty? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Falling poverty in India is increasingly a question of where the poor live and what work they do." Discuss.
parts: Where the poor live: regional concentration
What work they do: jobs and earnings

answer.t: The World Bank estimates India's extreme poverty fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, but about 57% of the remaining poor live in one belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal.

pts.t: Lagging states in the Gangetic plain hold most residual poverty, so national averages hide regional gaps.
pts.ex: The UP–West Bengal belt holds about 57% of the poor.

pts.t: These states have fewer manufacturing and urban jobs to absorb farm labour.
High population growth and young cohorts strain jobs and services.
Small holdings and flood-prone lands keep rural incomes low and volatile.
Lower investment, credit and connectivity limit enterprise.
Weaker delivery of health, education and schemes slows human-capital gains.
Jobs grew by 13.4 crore (2017-23), but mostly in low-productivity activities.
Rural women drove job growth, often in self-employment and unpaid family work.
The top 10% earn about 13 times the bottom 10%.
It rose from 14.6% to 15.9% in a year.
Most workers lack contracts and social security, so shocks push them back into poverty.
Education does not translate into productive jobs.
Industrial corridors, MSME clusters and agro-processing in the eastern belt.
Textiles, food processing and electronics assembly to absorb farm labour.
Apprenticeships linked with employers.
Childcare, safe transport and SHG credit to move women into better-paid work.
Portable benefits under the Code on Social Security.
Regular surveys that capture top incomes and earnings.

answer.t: With the poorest now concentrated in a few regions and in low-paid work, the next fall in poverty will come from productive jobs in the eastern belt, not from transfers alone.

title: The missing middle in India's growth story
syllabus: GS3 › Growth, development and employment; Inclusive growth; Infrastructure; Energy · GS1 › Effects of globalisation; Social stratification
summary: India has stayed lower-middle income for 19 years while Vietnam and China moved up fast; five statistics show jobs, factories, private investment, power and a thin middle class holding it back.
evolution: India enters the World Bank's lower-middle-income group.
Vietnam, lower-middle income since 2009, moves up to upper-middle income this year: about 16 years.
China moves from lower-middle to upper-middle income in 13 years.
India still lower-middle income, 19 years on; five countries move up this year.
ideas: Stuck in the middle: India has been lower-middle income for 19 years; Vietnam and China moved up in 16 and 13. At 8.5% dollar growth, against 5.4% in the past decade, India could get there in about six years.
GS3 · Growth / middle-income trap
Nineteen years after turning lower-middle income, India is still there, while Vietnam took 16 years and China 13 to move up.

Jobs without productivity: the labour force grew by 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women, mostly self-employed in farming; 43% still work in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal firms.
GS3 employment · GS1 women
Employment is not productive employment: 43% of India's workers remain in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers in informal enterprises.

Factories but no factory jobs: registered factories doubled, yet manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen; more workers joined the gig economy than formal manufacturing, and capital-intensive growth widened inequality.
GS3 · Manufacturing / inequality
Though registered factories doubled to 2.6 lakh, manufacturing has not become India's ladder of mass upward mobility.
Public investment has not crowded in private investment: infrastructure cut logistics costs, but firms repaired balance sheets and rewarded shareholders instead of investing.
GS3 · Investment
Public infrastructure spending was meant to crowd in private investment, but the private sector has not taken the baton.
Power is a binding constraint: solar has outrun storage and transmission, so output was curtailed even as demand peaked, hurting factories, data centres and AI.
GS3 · Energy / infrastructure
Solar generation running ahead of storage and transmission makes electricity a constraint on India's manufacturing and AI ambitions.
Rich faster than a middle class: 9.4 lakh dollar millionaires, but a broad middle class is not forming; premiumisation and capital outflows follow.
GS3 inclusive growth · GS1 inequality
India is producing millionaires faster than a broad middle class, the missing middle of its growth story.
keywords: Countries stuck at middle income, unable to move up
Without productive jobs, India risks a middle-income trap.
Workers moving from farms to factories and modern services
India's structural transformation has stalled: workers left farms for informal work, not factories.
Jobs with rising output and income per worker
Being employed is not the same as being productively employed.
Work that adds little output, taken because unemployment is unaffordable
The poor cannot afford to be unemployed, so low unemployment hides underemployment.
Public investment drawing in private investment
Public capex has not crowded in private investment.
Growth driven by machines more than labour
Capital-intensive manufacturing has raised profits faster than wages.
Premiumisation reflects growth concentrated at the top.
Women forming a growing share of farm work
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in farming.
data: Rise in India's labour force in less than a decade; two-thirds women
India's labour force grew by over 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women (World Bank).
Workforce still in agriculture / non-farm workers in informal enterprises
43% of India's workers are in agriculture, and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal enterprises.
Registered factories doubled from 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh, yet manufacturing's share stayed flat.
examples: Vietnam
Lower-middle income in 2009; moved up to upper-middle income this year, about 16 years later
Best practice: export-led manufacturing
Vietnam moved from lower- to upper-middle income in 16 years, a model of manufacturing-led growth.
China
Upper-middle income in 2010, 13 years after becoming lower-middle
Best practice: factory-led mobility
China reached upper-middle income in just 13 years by putting workers on factory floors.
Solar curtailment, summer 2026
Solar output cut despite peak demand, for lack of storage and transmission
Energy constraint
In summer 2026, India curtailed solar power even at peak demand for lack of storage and grid.
pyqs: India skipped the manufacturing stage; the missing middle is the result.
Jobs grew with the labour force, but not productive jobs.
Manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive: factories doubled, factory jobs did not.
Industrial growth lagging GDP: manufacturing's share has not risen.
Growth led by more labour, not productivity: the 100 million new workers are mostly in low-value work.
Manufacturing's share in GDP and MSMEs: the core of the missing middle.
Infrastructure investment has cut logistics costs but not yet crowded in private investment.

trend.t: UPSC has asked the same structural question for a decade: India moved from agriculture to services and skipped manufacturing (2014), growth has been jobless (2015), manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive (2017) and growth rests on more labour, not productivity (2022). The latest questions ask for solutions: manufacturing and MSMEs (2023) and labour codes (2024).
trend.watch: Manufacturing and productive employment have come in 2014, 2017 (twice), 2022 and 2023. Structural transformation is a must-study area in GS3.
focus: Manufacturing-led jobs: PLI, MSMEs, labour-intensive sectors
Crowding in private investment after public capex
Power, storage and transmission as constraints on industry
Inequality and the middle class; women's productive employment

potential: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale. (15 marks)
Why has manufacturing not become the engine of employment in India despite the rise in registered factories? Examine. (10 marks)
Public investment in infrastructure has not crowded in private investment. Analyse the reasons and suggest measures. (10 marks)
India is producing millionaires faster than a broad middle class. Examine the implications for inclusive growth. (10 marks)

practice.q: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale.
parts: Introduction: India's 19 years at lower-middle income vs Vietnam and China (one line, with facts)
Strategy for high-productivity jobs (way forward, its own part)

answer.t: India has been lower-middle income since 2007, while Vietnam moved up in 16 years and China in 13 (World Bank).

pts.t: Workers moved from farms into informal work, not factories.
pts.ex: 43% still in agriculture; 79% of non-farm workers informal.

pts.t: Factories doubled, but manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen.
pts.ex: 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh registered factories, 2004-05 to 2024-25.

pts.t: Machines over labour keep wages behind profits and raise inequality.
Firms deleveraged and paid shareholders instead of building capacity, despite public capex.
Solar outruns storage and transmission, so supply is unreliable.
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in agriculture.
Many workers lack skills for modern manufacturing and services.
Wealth concentrates at the top, limiting broad-based demand.
Prioritise textiles, apparel, footwear, electronics assembly and food processing.
Tie incentives to employment, not just output.
Credit, technology and easier compliance.
Predictable policy, faster clearances and demand certainty.
Storage, transmission and reliable, affordable supply.
Vocational training, childcare and safe transport to bring women into factories.
Flexibility for firms with social security for workers.

answer.t: India can escape the middle-income trap only by moving its workers from low- to high-productivity jobs, with public infrastructure and private capital working together.

title: Govt to study hurdles faced by women-led informal businesses
syllabus: GS1 › Role of women; Women's issues · GS3 › Employment; Inclusive growth
context: The Statistics Ministry plans to add questions to its Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) on 'women-specific constraints' such as restrictions on time and mobility and household responsibilities.
ideas: What is not measured is rarely fixed; better data is the first step to targeted support for women entrepreneurs.
GS1 women · GS3 inclusive growth
What is not measured is rarely fixed; MoSPI's new survey questions are a first step to supporting women entrepreneurs.
Household and care responsibilities hold back women's work; the gap is widest among the young.
GS3 · Female LFPR
Household and care duties hold back women's work most among the young.
keywords: Too little free time because of unpaid work
Time poverty from unpaid care work keeps India's women out of paid work.
Household and care work that is not paid or counted
Unpaid care work remains invisible in GDP but sustains the economy.
Gender-disaggregated data is the basis of gender-responsive policy.
Share of women working or looking for work
India's female LFPR, at 34.6% against 77.4% for men (PLFS), shows the gender gap in work.
data: Female vs male labour force participation (Sept)
Women's labour force participation is 34.6% against 77.4% for men (PLFS, September).
Among 15–29-year-olds, women's participation is just 21.5% against 61.1% for men.
About 27% of India's informal enterprises are headed by women (ASUSE 2025).
examples: MoSPI's gender-responsive survey
Adding women-specific questions to a national survey
Good governance
MoSPI's adding women-specific constraints to its enterprise survey shows the state measuring before it fixes.
pyqs: Measuring household responsibilities makes the care burden on women entrepreneurs visible.
Use the LFPR gap (34.6% women vs 77.4% men) to show equity needs targeted support.
27% of informal enterprises are headed by women; informality shapes their constraints.
summary: The Statistics Ministry will add questions on women-specific constraints (time, mobility, household duties) to its survey of informal businesses.
evolution: First Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE).
Latest round: 27% of informal enterprises women-headed.
